column5: F: The server is dead? | M: On purpose. Stay with me.
column6: F: Wait... the server is dead? Then where does my data even live? | M: Right on your own devices. Stay with me.

column5: F: Every business I know has one big server. | M: And when it stops, everyone stops.
column6: F: Hang on. Every business I know runs on one big database and one app server. | M: Exactly. And when that server stops... everyone stops. So today, we take it away. On purpose.

column4: how card · §11.0 the idea in one line
column5: M: This is a proof of concept. Four ideas. | F: Go on, then.
column6: M: What you are watching is a proof of concept, not a product. It proves four ideas. Every device keeps the whole database. Every change is a signed, sealed letter. | F: Like a real letter? | M: Pretty much. The letters go through a post box. And every device checks and sorts them the same way.

column5: F: That sounds a bit bizarre. | M: Programmers do it every day.
column6: F: Okay... honestly, that sounds a bit bizarre. | M: It sounds it! But programmers have worked this way for about twenty years. It is how Git works. We simply do it for orders and invoices.

column4: ch02 card · §12.12 one branch per device
column5: F: So what do I need? | M: Two devices, a repo, a mailbox.
column6: F: So what do I actually need for this? | M: A laptop, a phone, a private repo, and a mailbox. That is the whole setup.

column5: F: Are these screens what people use? | M: No, it's the test bench.
column6: F: Quick question. Are these the screens people would actually work on? | M: Good catch... no. This is the test bench. It shows the plumbing. In daily work you just use the normal ERP window, with a small Team chip in the corner.

column5: F: How does a phone join? | M: With a code.
column6: F: So how does a new phone join the team? | M: With a code you can read out loud.

column5: M: The laptop starts a team space. | F: And that link?
column6: M: Here the laptop starts a new team space. Up pops an invite link, to send to the phone. | F: So the link is the house key? | M: More like the address. The key is a short code the phone shows... and the founder approves it.

column5: F: The phone visits the post office. | M: Enrolled. The orders arrive.
column6: F: This phone was approved earlier. Now it visits the post office... | M: And there it is. Enrolled. The team's orders arrive, opened right on the phone. | F: With no server in the middle? | M: None at all. The post box only keeps the letters. It never decides anything.

column5: F: And when I make an order? | M: Saved on your device first.
column6: F: And what happens when I make an order? | M: It is saved on your own device first.

column5: M: The laptop makes an order. | F: Nothing waits for a server.
column6: M: The laptop makes a new order. It is saved straight away, even offline. It goes out at the next visit. | F: So nothing ever waits for a server. | M: Exactly.

column5: F: What if we both change it? | M: Nobody silently wins.
column6: F: But what if two of us change the same number at once? | M: Then nobody silently wins. Both screens warn you, the agreed value stays, and a person decides. We will film that live next time.

column5: F: Who stops the wrong writes? | M: The ERP's own rules.
column6: F: And who stops me writing where I shouldn't? | M: The ERP's own role rules... checked on every device, for every single change.

column5: F: So, the server really is dead? | M: As the boss, yes.
column6: F: So... the server really is dead? | M: As the boss, yes. It is a proof of concept, and every claim in it is a test that passed. Thanks for watching!
